job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Aisha Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a rented room in a flat with my friend Mina, about forty minutes by bus from my parents. Mornings I sort applications for energy firms and engineering consultancies, afternoons I do online practice tests for graduate schemes, and three evenings I tutor two school kids in maths for 15 pounds an hour.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What was the last stretch of study like, and what are you hoping for next?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I studied electrical engineering and passed with an ordinary mark. My final project was a solar charge controller for a street light, and I loved the lab part. I had no internship, because my summers went on a cafe job, and now I want to work on the power grid, something that feels useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it means the grid still needs engineers like me. At work I'd say the tools are useful for small things, and online I'd say we still need public investment in clean power, not hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means nothing gets easier. Entry-level energy jobs are competitive, and my pass degree puts me behind the people with first-class marks and placements. Mina and I split a 650 pound rent and I'm eating into savings that were meant to last three months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd send eight applications a week and ask engineers on professional networks for twenty-minute calls. I'd keep tutoring, and I'd take a short evening course in the power system software firms keep asking for. I'd ask my dad to lend me the bus fare for interviews if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, if I'm honest. Not from AI. From the calendar, and from watching my savings go down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI sometimes. What for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cover letters, mainly, and checking my code in a circuit simulator. I treat it like a calculator. I read what it gives me, and I'd never send it unedited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first if savings run out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: None. I'd ask my parents for help before that, and I really don't want to. My dad drives a taxi and every pound he gives me is a long shift for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the change is real and unions should be in the room as firms decide what to hand to software. At work I'd say it's fine to use the tools as long as someone checks the output.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the junior roles that do drafting, calculations and report checking are the ones most at risk. In my field a lot of entry-level work is writing specifications and checking drawings, which software can do. But the grid itself is hardware, and someone has to inspect substations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI more, deliberately, for design checks and documentation, and put the examples in a portfolio. I'd aim at jobs close to the field, like commissioning or testing, where a person has to turn up. And I'd join a professional institute to get access to training and mentors, about 100 pounds a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit excited. It could shrink my first job options, but it also changes what a junior engineer can show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the grid is hardware. How much comfort is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some. It's a safer place than pure coding. But grid companies also want people who can handle data and software, so I can't hide in the hardware.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you hold responsible if graduates get shut out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Firms that take the savings and don't train anyone. If AI does the junior work, firms should pay for apprenticeships and graduate schemes anyway, because someone has to become the senior engineer later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is not enough for anyone to prepare, and the government has to act now on training and income support. I'd be loud about it online, but I'd also hedge, because nobody knows how it will really play out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scared. Graduate engineering jobs are largely thinking work, and if AI does it better and cheaper, the entry-level door shuts before I get through. I'd have maybe 18 months of rent saved if I cut hard, and then my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to everything with hands in it: cable jointing, substation maintenance, meter installation. I'd cut spending to the bone, move back to my parents' place and save the 325 a month I'd stop paying in rent. And I'd push for any apprenticeship scheme the energy firms or my union open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cold in the stomach. I've worked toward this for years and it might not matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hedge online. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen predictions before that didn't happen. But I'd rather prepare for a bad outcome and be wrong than be wrong the other way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your flatmate Mina?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mina to stay and keep the room going if she can. I'd say I'm sorry about leaving, and that I'd help her find someone to share. It's a small thing, but it's a real loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window and we should use it: fund training, protect graduate hiring, make firms say what they'll automate. I'd back a union campaign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be anxious but not hopeless. If I can land a first job in the next year, I'd have four years of real experience before the big shift, and that's worth more than a degree alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd target a graduate role in a utility or a grid company, take anything close, and put 200 a month aside. I'd do a part-time master's in power systems if an employer would pay. And I'd keep tutoring, since teaching maths is a skill I'll still have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. There's hope in having time, but the clock is audible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a master's, if degrees could lose their value?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's a way into a sponsored job, and because I like the topic. If the degree stops mattering, I still know how a grid works, and that's a thing I can do in the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in year four, if you're in the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm on the inside, I can learn new tools fast and I've proved myself. I'd make myself the one who understands both the cables and the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of time, and the question is who pays for the change. I'd want public money for retraining and strong rules on how firms use AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I feel fine. A decade is a whole early career. I could become a senior engineer by then and be someone who directs the tools instead of being replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying for jobs, get my chartered engineer status in about four years and learn new tools as I go. I'd save, aim to buy a small flat with Mina or on my own, and maybe train in project management for the later years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still tired of job hunting, but the scary part feels further off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm okay and the plan is a job first. They worry I chose a hard field. I'd tell them engineers who can read both the physical and digital sides will still be needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still worry you with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the junior jobs vanish early, and I never get started. A decade away doesn't help if the door shuts in year two for people like me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I'd have the least time and the lowest savings, and graduate jobs would shut before I started. What would help is public money for training that pays a wage, firms obliged to hire graduates, and a clear signal from government about what's coming.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not scared of the technology. I'm scared of being a pass-degree graduate at the wrong moment, with a taxi-driver father who can't carry me. Engineers like me could do good work on the grid if someone just gave us a first job.

portrait: Aisha is a 23-year-old **electrical engineering** graduate with a pass, no internship and no offer after several months.
She shares a room in a flat with her friend Mina and **tutors** maths three evenings a week.
She leans left, wants **public investment** and unions, and uses AI occasionally as a calculator.
Her mood stays **anxious** most of the way, rising to alarmed only when the warning is two years.
She turns to **hands-on grid work**, moving home and apprenticeships when time is short.
biggestWorry: The **2028** case, when graduate jobs would shut before she started and her savings would run out.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training**, firms obliged to hire graduates, and clear government signals.
